vignette:
Darnell, a 27-year-old African American man who drove a taxi and Uber in the city, described his childhood in a way that still seemed organized around one house, one man, and one kind of fear. His caregiver had beaten him regularly as a boy, and Darnell could remember the body of it with painful clarity: the rough texture of the couch fabric under his hands while he waited to be grabbed, the sting of a particular coldness on his skin when he was forced to stand in an unheated hallway, and the sound of heavy footsteps coming down behind him when he thought he had made it to his room. Those sensations had become potent cues in adulthood. When a passenger slid into the back seat and his clothing brushed the upholstery in a certain way, or when he heard footsteps approaching his car from behind at night, his chest tightened and he became instantly alert, scanning mirrors and checking locks. In those moments he tended to distract himself with music, phone scrolling, or by taking one more fare when he was already tired, and he also drank and used drugs more than he intended, telling himself he needed something to blunt the jolt.

Over time, Darnell had come to believe that his body had not caught up with his life. He said it felt like it kept reacting as if danger were still present, even when he was safe, and that made him feel permanently changed for the worse. He spoke with shame about feeling cut off from his community and culture, as if the abuse had separated him from an ease with other people that other men seemed to have. Those beliefs shaped what he did next. Because he was certain something inside him had been damaged, he pulled away from emotional closeness and avoided intimacy, keeping relationships casual and brief. He also leaned on distraction and drugs to get through evenings after work, and the more he numbed himself, the more he noticed how distant he felt from others and from himself, which reinforced the sense that he no longer belonged anywhere. That belief did not stay abstract; it colored his view of every tense conversation, every invitation to get close, and every quiet moment in which he felt the ache of being on the outside of his own life.

At the same time, Darnell lived as if danger could appear without warning. He was hypervigilant in traffic and at street corners, checking over his shoulder even when no one was there, and he could not trust safety even when passengers, friends, or family told him he was fine. He described taking too many risks on the road and in his personal life, partly because he felt he had to stay in control by moving fast and staying busy, and partly because he seemed to accept harm as inevitable. These habits fed back into his beliefs: when he found himself needing another high, avoiding a call from someone who wanted more closeness, or jumping at a set of footsteps behind him on the sidewalk, it felt to him like proof that the damage was permanent and that his body was still wired for attack. The more he arranged his life around keeping watch and keeping others at a distance, the less comfort he got from people, and the more he concluded that connection was no longer available to him.

The original memories remained active because present-day cues kept reawakening them. In the cramped back seat of his own car, the rough feel of a seat cover, a sudden blast of cold air on his forearm from an open window, or footsteps approaching the driver's side at a pickup could pull him straight back into childhood without warning. Once those moments struck, he would intensify his guard, avoid eye contact, keep conversations flat, and sometimes use drugs after a shift to come down. His avoidance made the cues more charged, because the less he tolerated closeness or ordinary bodily discomfort, the more startling the sensations became when they returned. Darnell eventually sought help after a close call in which he drove recklessly while exhausted and high, then realized he had no real memory of the last few miles. What frightened him most was not only that he might get himself hurt, but that he might stay trapped in this state forever; what he hoped for was some way to feel safe in his body again without having to live cut off from people, work, and the life he still wanted.
